### Summary The change-request approval HTML email template renders fields as raw HTML. User who can create a change request can inject HTML into approval notification emails. I was not able to confirm Enterprise platform is using vulnerable code nor that it doesn't sanitize input. ### Details `src/mailtemplates/requested-cr-approval/requested-cr-approval.html.mustache` uses Mustache triple-stash syntax for fields that can originate from users: ```mustache {{{ changeRequestTitle }}} {{{ requesterName }}} {{{ requesterEmail }}} {{{ changeRequestLink }}} ``` Triple-stash disables HTML escaping even when Mustache's global escape function is safe. The related renderer is `sendRequestedCRApprovalEmail` in `src/lib/services/email-service.ts`, which renders the template with `Mustache.render`. ### PoC 1. Use an Enterprise deployment with change requests and approval emails enabled. 2. As a project member who can create change requests, set a display name or change-request title to HTML such as: ```html Approve change request ``` 3. Create a change request that requires approval. 4. Observe that the approval email contains attacker-controlled raw HTML instead of escaped text. ### Impact Change-request approvers can receive forged links, tracking pixels, or visually altered email content.

cwe.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

cves.summary:
## Summary

The `@novu/js` In-App Inbox renderer passes a notification's `redirect.url` to `window.open()` with no URL-scheme validation. The value originates from a notification's call-to-action and is delivered to the recipient verbatim.

An authenticated organization member (or any holder of the environment API key) creates a v1 in-app workflow whose step CTA stores `cta.data = { url: "javascript:<payload>", target: "_self" }`. The v1 message-template `cta.data` field is a Mongoose `Mixed` type, so the arbitrary `target` key is accepted and persisted. The server-side inbox mapper copies `cta.data.url` and `cta.data.target` into the notification's `redirect` object with no scheme check. Novu's v2 control schema validates redirect URLs against `redirectUrlRegex` (which rejects `javascript:`), proving the intended invariant; the v1 path and the client renderer do not enforce it.

When the recipient clicks the notification, the inbox calls `window.open(url, "_self", "noopener noreferrer")`. In Chromium browsers a `javascript:` URL opened with `target="_self"` executes in the current document origin (the default `_blank` is browser-blocked, so the attacker sets `_self`).

Result: a low-privilege content author runs arbitrary JavaScript in the browser of every recipient who clicks, in the origin that hosts the inbox (the customer application or the self-hosted Novu dashboard, neither of which sends a CSP).

## Affected

novuhq/novu self-hosted and cloud, API <= v3.15.0; `@novu/js` <= 3.15.0 and `@novu/react` (Inbox component). Confirmed live-exploitable on v3.15.0 (Docker community compose, default config, default roles).
Condition: an in-app (Inbox) channel is in use, the standard product configuration.
Recipient must use a Chromium-based browser (Chrome, Edge); the `javascript:` execution does not occur where the browser blocks `javascript:` in `window.open`.

## Root cause

packages/js/src/ui/context/InboxContext.tsx:108: `window.open(url, target ?? DEFAULT_TARGET, DEFAULT_REFERRER)` is reached for any URL not starting with `/`, with no scheme allowlist, so `javascript:` is passed through.
packages/js/src/ui/components/Notification/DefaultNotification.tsx:103: the notification click handler calls `navigate(redirect.url, redirect.target)`, feeding the stored values into the sink.
apps/api/src/app/inbox/utils/notification-mapper.ts:85-89: maps `cta.data.url` and `cta.data.target` into `redirect` with no validation of either field.
libs/dal/src/repositories/message-template/message-template.schema.ts:41: `data: Schema.Types.Mixed` accepts the arbitrary `target` key (not present in the typed interface).
libs/application-generic/src/usecases/compile-in-app-template/compile-in-app-template.usecase.ts:35-36: the v1 render path handlebars-compiles `cta.data.url` and performs no scheme check.
libs/application-generic/src/schemas/control/in-app-control.schema.ts:24-27: the v2 control schema enforces `url: z.string().regex(redirectUrlRegex)` which rejects `javascript:`, the guard absent from the v1 path and the renderer.

## Reproduction

novuhq/novu v3.15.0 Docker community compose, default config. Attacker holds an environment API key (or a member session); victim opens the inbox in Chromium.

1. Create a v1 in-app workflow with a redirect CTA carrying a `javascript:` URL and `target=_self`:
```
POST /v1/workflows   Authorization: ApiKey <key>
{"name":"poc","notificationGroupId":"<ng>","active":true,
 "steps":[{"template":{"type":"in_app","content":"click me",
   "cta":{"type":"redirect","data":{
     "url":"javascript:window.top.__X=document.domain;void 0","target":"_self"}}}}]}
```
2. Trigger it to a subscriber, then read the feed with a subscriber token minted from the public application identifier (no secret):
```
POST /v1/inbox/session {"applicationIdentifier":"<appId>","subscriberId":"<sub>"}
GET  /v1/inbox/notifications   Authorization: Bearer <subscriber-jwt>
-> redirect: {"url":"javascript:window.top.__X=document.domain;void 0","target":"_self"}
```
3. The subscriber clicks the notification in the `@novu/js` / `@novu/react` Inbox.

Live-verified: the stored `javascript:` URL is returned verbatim by the inbox feed, and the exact shipped `navigate()` logic invoked from a real click runs `window.open(url,"_self",...)`, executing the payload in the `http://<dashboard>:4000` origin (no CSP); `window.top.__X` was set to the page origin. On the self-hosted dashboard the test inbox bell uses `subscriberId = user.externalId` (apps/dashboard/src/components/inbox-button.tsx:102), so a member targets another member's id and the executing payload reads `localStorage['self-hosted-jwt']` (apps/dashboard/src/utils/self-hosted/jwt-manager.tsx:4), the dashboard session token.

## Impact

- Stored XSS in the recipient's browser, cross-principal (content author to end-user subscriber), persistent, replicated to every recipient of the workflow.
- On the self-hosted dashboard origin (no CSP), theft of `localStorage['self-hosted-jwt']` yields takeover of another member or admin account.
- In a customer application embedding the inbox, session and token theft and authenticated actions in that origin.
- Triggered by the lowest privilege that can author a workflow, default config, one recipient click.

## Credit

Jan Kahmen, [turingpoint](https://turingpoint.de) (jan@turingpoint.de)

cves.summary:
## Impact

The undici WebSocket client enforces `maxPayloadSize` on the cumulative byte count of fragments in a message but does not enforce a limit on the number of fragments. A malicious WebSocket server can stream many small or empty continuation frames that each pass per-frame and cumulative-size validation, collectively causing unbounded memory growth in the client process. The result is memory exhaustion and a denial of service.

Affected applications are those using the undici WebSocket client (`new WebSocket(...)`) or the `WebSocketStream` API that can be induced to connect to an attacker-controlled or compromised WebSocket endpoint.

All releases starting at undici 6.17.0 are affected.

## Patches

Upgrade to undici v6.27.0, v7.28.0 or v8.5.0.

## Workarounds

No workaround is available. The fix must be applied through an upgrade.

A vulnerability was identified in Linksys E5600 1.1.0.26. Affected by this vulnerability is the function strcpy of the file /cgi-bin/mesh_login.cgi of the component JSON Request Parser. The manipulation of the argument username/password/token/source/cn/action leads to out-of-bounds write. The attack may be initiated remotely. The exploit is publicly available and might be used. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond in any way. This vulnerability only affects products that are no longer supported by the maintainer.

@better-auth/expo before 1.7.16 allows certain account-takeover outcomes (e.g., unauthenticated changes of any account's email address), because it signs a caller-supplied state value without checking whether that value had been issued by the server. NOTE: the application secret must be rotated after updating to a fixed version.

A weakness has been identified in Linksys E5600 1.1.0.26. This affects an unknown part of the file /cgi-bin/fqc.cgi of the component Factory Quality Control. This manipulation causes information disclosure. Remote exploitation of the attack is possible. The exploit has been made available to the public and could be used for attacks. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond in any way. This vulnerability only affects products that are no longer supported by the maintainer.

The ActiveX control for invoking a scriptlet in Internet Explorer 5.0 through 5.5 renders arbitrary file types instead of HTML, which allows an attacker to read arbitrary files, aka a variant of the "Scriptlet Rendering" vulnerability.
glFTPD 1.23 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (CPU consumption) via a LIST command with an argument that contains a large number of * (asterisk) characters.

The admin.html file in StepWeb Search Engine (SWS) 2.5 stores passwords in links to manager.pl, which allows remote attackers who can access the admin.html file to gain administrative privileges to SWS.
ServerMask 2.2 and earlier does not obfuscate (1) ETag, (2) HTTP Status Message, or (3) Allow HTTP responses, which could tell remote attackers that the web server is an IIS server.

Under certain circumstances, private (non-exported) `query.batch` functions could end up sharing a batch, resulting in the arguments from one function being passed to another. This only affects apps using the experimental remote functions flag and non-exported `query.batch` functions.

If an attacker could, using some form of social engineering or other exploit, get a user to use client-side navigation to navigate to a specially-crafted link, the attacker could cause code from another domain to be imported and run on the user's machine. This only affected apps with `router.resolution: 'server'`.

cwe.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation

cves.summary:
## Summary

`nltk.sem.chat80.sql_query()` opens a SQLite database by handing the result of `nltk.data.find(dbname)` straight to `sqlite3.connect()` without the path-containment check that the NLTK data sandbox (`nltk.pathsec`) is meant to enforce. `nltk.data.find()` applies only lexical checks to the resource name and returns a `FileSystemPathPointer` whose path is normalized with `os.path.abspath` but never resolved for symlinks. As a result, an in-root symbolic link that points at a SQLite file outside every registered NLTK data root is followed by SQLite, and the caller receives query results from the out-of-sandbox database. An attacker who can place a file inside a directory the application trusts as an NLTK data root can read SQLite databases that the pathsec sandbox is supposed to keep out of reach.

## Root Cause

The security invariant is that file access performed through NLTK data resolution must stay within the configured data roots; the sandbox enforces this in `nltk.pathsec` via `validate_path` and `pathsec.open`, which resolve the real path (`Path(...).resolve()`) and reject targets outside the allowed roots. `sql_query()` never reaches that enforcement point. It calls `nltk.data.find(dbname)`, whose guards operate purely on the resource-name string, and `FileSystemPathPointer.__init__` performs only `os.path.abspath` plus an existence check, which does not collapse symlinks. The pointer is then passed to `sqlite3.connect(str(path))`, so the containment decision that `FileSystemPathPointer.open()` would delegate to `pathsec.open` is bypassed entirely. The sibling functions in the same module that create or write databases (`cities2table`, `val_dump`, `val_load`) obtain their protection from a validation call in later development, but the read sink `sql_query` performs no equivalent check in any published release.

```text
nltk/sem/chat80.py  -> sql_query(): path = nltk.data.find(dbname); sqlite3.connect(str(path))
nltk/data.py        -> find(): lexical name guards only; returns FileSystemPathPointer
nltk/data.py        -> FileSystemPathPointer.__init__(): os.path.abspath + os.path.exists (no symlink resolution)
nltk/data.py        -> FileSystemPathPointer.open() -> nltk.pathsec.open (the containment guard that sql_query never calls)
```

## Impact

An attacker who can write into a directory the application registers as an NLTK data root (a shared or writable corpus directory, or a downloaded corpus) can plant a symbolic link at the expected resource location that points at a SQLite database elsewhere on the filesystem. When the application invokes `sql_query()` (directly or via `sql_demo()`) for that resource, SQLite follows the link and the query executes against the out-of-sandbox database, returning its rows to the caller. This escapes the pathsec confidentiality boundary. The read primitive is bounded to SQLite-format files that are readable by the process user: a non-SQLite target raises `sqlite3.DatabaseError` rather than leaking content. A caller-supplied write query would be redirected onto the out-of-sandbox target and SQLite may create sidecar files (`-wal`, `-journal`) next to it, which is a plausible integrity side effect rather than a demonstrated arbitrary-write primitive. Exploitation requires the same local write capability into a trusted data root as the related symlink-read sandbox-escape issues already recorded for this project.

## Proof of Concept

`Requires the published nltk 3.10.3 wheel and a writable directory registered as an NLTK data root. No network access is needed.`

1. Create a throwaway data root with the expected corpus subdirectory.
2. Create a SQLite database outside that root and populate it.
3. Plant an in-root symbolic link at `corpora/city_database/city.db` pointing at the outside database.
4. Register the data root and call `sql_query()` for the in-root resource name.

```python
import os, tempfile, sqlite3, nltk, nltk.data
from nltk.sem import chat80

work = tempfile.mkdtemp()
root = os.path.join(work, "nltk_data")
corp = os.path.join(root, "corpora", "city_database")
os.makedirs(corp)

secret = os.path.join(work, "outside", "secret.db")
os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(secret))
con = sqlite3.connect(secret)
con.execute("CREATE TABLE t (x text)")
con.execute("INSERT INTO t VALUES ('OUT-OF-SANDBOX-SECRET')")
con.commit(); con.close()

os.symlink(secret, os.path.join(corp, "city.db"))
nltk.data.path.insert(0, root)

ptr = nltk.data.find("corpora/city_database/city.db")
try:
    ptr.open().read()            # pathsec route: blocked
except Exception as e:
    print("open() blocked:", type(e).__name__)

cur = chat80.sql_query("corpora/city_database/city.db", "SELECT * FROM t")
print("sql_query rows:", cur.fetchall())   # sink route: follows the symlink
```

```text
open() blocked: PermissionError
sql_query rows: [('OUT-OF-SANDBOX-SECRET',)]
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** The application exposes `sql_query()` (or `sql_demo()`, which calls it) and resolves the target database through `nltk.data.find`, using at least one directory the attacker can write to as a data root.
2. **Control:** The attacker controls the on-disk object at the in-root resource path, replacing it with a symbolic link whose target is chosen freely. The resource-name argument stays a clean, in-root string.
3. **Path:** `nltk.data.find` applies its lexical name guards (`_UNSAFE_NO_PROTOCOL_RE`, encoded and normalized-form checks), which inspect only the name string and pass, then returns a `FileSystemPathPointer` whose `__init__` applies `os.path.abspath` and an existence check without resolving the symlink.
4. **Guard:** The containment guard (`FileSystemPathPointer.open()` delegating to `nltk.pathsec.open`, which resolves the real path and rejects out-of-root targets) is never invoked, because `sql_query()` passes the raw pointer string to `sqlite3.connect()` instead of opening through the pointer.
5. **Primitive:** `sqlite3.connect(str(path))` opens the symlink target; the kernel follows the link out of every data root and the cursor executes the query against the outside database.
6. **Result:** Rows from a SQLite database outside the sandbox are returned to the caller, escaping the pathsec confidentiality boundary for SQLite-format files readable by the process user.

## Bypass Evidence

The relevant guard is the pathsec containment enforced by `nltk.pathsec.open`/`validate_path`, reached through `FileSystemPathPointer.open()`. On an identical pointer produced from the planted symlink, `ptr.open()` raises `PermissionError` with an "Unauthorized path" security violation, confirming the guard is active and correct for the sandbox route. `sql_query()` does not call `.open()` and does not call `validate_path`; it passes the unresolved pointer string directly to `sqlite3.connect()`, so the guard never runs on this path and the read succeeds. Attempts to invalidate the finding were made and failed: `nltk.data.find` was checked for a hidden containment or real-path resolution and has none (its guards are name-string only, and `FileSystemPathPointer.__init__` uses `abspath`, not `realpath`); SQLite was confirmed to follow the link and read the outside file rather than opening the link node; and the possibility that an existing published fix already covers this sink was refuted by inspecting the published artifacts, where no containment check is present on `sql_query`. The behavior was reproduced against the exact published 3.10.3 wheel (verified by its published SHA-256 digest).

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: PyPI`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 3.9.4, <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, wheel SHA-256 ff9598a8e20518ee0d557745890cc4435b9578489e2dcbc69c4f81fa060caf7c)`
- `Fix status: 3.10.4`

The pathsec sandbox that this issue bypasses was introduced in 3.9.4; the immediately preceding release 3.9.3 does not ship `nltk/pathsec.py` and therefore does not present this sandbox-escape surface. Every published release from 3.9.4 through the current latest 3.10.3 ships `nltk/pathsec.py` with `ENFORCE = True` and ships `sql_query()` without any containment check, so all of them are affected. Each affected wheel was fetched from PyPI and inspected directly. No published release removes the sink or adds the guard, so no fixed version exists at the time of review.

## Suggested Fix

Enforce the data-root containment invariant on the resolved database path before opening it. In `sql_query()`, validate the path through the same mechanism the sibling functions use (for example `validate_path(str(path), context="chat80.sql_query")`) or open the database through the pointer's sandboxed open path rather than passing the raw string to `sqlite3.connect()`. The remediation should resolve symbolic links (real-path resolution) and reject targets outside the registered data roots, and it should cover any other read sinks that connect to on-disk databases resolved through `nltk.data.find`. As an interim mitigation, applications should ensure that no attacker-writable directory is registered as an NLTK data root and should avoid calling `sql_query`/`sql_demo` on resources that live in shared or untrusted locations.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

## Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: IN PROGRESS (fix on an open pull request, not yet on develop).

PR: #3888 "Validate chat80.sql_query dbname for path containment (CWE-59/73)", open; head e0e890f51 at the time of this note. This is the same sink and vector as GHSA-xv54-447f-mj22 (now closed).

Fix commits: 9f5d2ea6d (sql_query calls validate_path before nltk.data.find, as cities2table, val_dump and val_load already do) and 47bd0476e (the file behind a sql_query resource name is resolved through the data roots and validated, and its store is pinned).

The advisory PoC (an in-root corpora/city_database/city.db symlink to an out-of-root SQLite file, resolved through find()) re-run on the PR head e0e890f51: refused with PermissionError (Security Violation [chat80.sql_query]: Unauthorized path, naming the symlink's resolved out-of-root target); the same resource name backed by a real in-root database still returns its rows on that head. On develop 2fa3f48fe the PoC returns the rows of the out-of-root database, so develop is VULNERABLE.

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_xv54_447f_mj22.py on the PR (the sibling advisory GHSA-xv54-447f-mj22), FIXED on the PR head (absolute path, traversal and a symlink inside a scratch directory are all security-rejected). Those three cases are also rejected on develop by find() itself; the in-root symlink above is the case that only the PR closes.

Release: none.

cwe.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory

cves.summary:
### Summary
Path traversal in NLTK's save_maxent_params() and load_maxent_params() allows arbitrary file write and arbitrary file read outside the directories permitted by NLTK's pathsec security mechanism.

This vulnerability was previously reported through Huntr, accepted by the NLTK project, and assigned CVE-2026-15367. A $750 bounty was paid through Huntr (i didnt get the fix bounty). Huntr subsequently shut down its OSS vulnerability program, so I am submitting this report through GitHub to continue the existing disclosure process and preserve the original CVE assignment and researcher credit.

### Details
The affected functions are:

- nltk.classify.maxent.load_maxent_params()
- nltk.classify.maxent.save_maxent_params()

Both functions construct filesystem paths from the caller-controlled tab_dir argument and access them using Python's built-in open() without passing the paths through NLTK's pathsec validation.

For example, load_maxent_params() constructs and opens:

- <tab_dir>/weights.txt
- <tab_dir>/mapping.tab
- <tab_dir>/labels.txt
- <tab_dir>/alwayson.tab

Similarly, save_maxent_params() creates/writes files under the supplied tab_dir.

This bypasses the security boundary provided by nltk.pathsec. NLTK documents pathsec as the mechanism for restricting filesystem access to permitted roots, with strict enforcement intended to prevent unauthorized filesystem access.

The relevant implementation is in:

nltk/classify/maxent.py

The affected functions can be found in the model parameter loading/saving section of that file.

This issue was previously disclosed through Huntr and accepted before the Huntr OSS program was shut down. The original Huntr report was assigned CVE-2026-15367 and received a $750 bounty.

I am therefore submitting this GitHub Security Advisory primarily as a continuation/transfer of the existing disclosure rather than as a new vulnerability report.

### PoC
The issue can be reproduced by enabling NLTK's path security enforcement and supplying a tab_dir outside the permitted root.

For example, with a controlled test environment:

```py
import os
import tempfile
import nltk.pathsec as pathsec
from nltk.classify.maxent import load_maxent_params, save_maxent_params

pathsec.ENFORCE = True

allowed_dir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
outside_dir = tempfile.mkdtemp()

# The same outside-root path is rejected when accessed through pathsec.
try:
    with pathsec.open(os.path.join(outside_dir, "test.txt"), "w") as f:
        f.write("test")
except Exception as e:
    print("pathsec.open rejected outside-root access:", type(e).__name__)

# The vulnerable model-parameter APIs directly use open()
# on paths derived from tab_dir.
#
# Supplying outside_dir as tab_dir causes the functions to access
# files under outside_dir rather than enforcing the pathsec boundary.
```

For save_maxent_params(), the attacker-controlled tab_dir determines where the model parameter files are written.

For load_maxent_params(), the attacker-controlled tab_dir determines which files are read.

The important security property being bypassed is that pathsec.ENFORCE = True does not protect these file operations because the affected functions call the built-in open() directly rather than the pathsec-aware file-opening mechanism.

### Impact
This is a path traversal / filesystem sandbox bypass resulting in arbitrary local file read and arbitrary local file write.

Applications that use NLTK's pathsec mechanism as a filesystem security boundary may incorrectly assume that model parameter loading and saving are restricted to approved directories.

An attacker who can influence the tab_dir argument may therefore:

- read files outside the permitted NLTK data directories through load_maxent_params();
- create or overwrite files outside the permitted directories through save_maxent_params();
- bypass the filesystem containment provided by nltk.pathsec.

The practical impact depends on how an application exposes these APIs and what filesystem permissions the NLTK process has.

### Existing CVE / Disclosure History

CVE: CVE-2026-15367

This vulnerability was previously reported and accepted through Huntr before the Huntr OSS vulnerability program was shut down. The report received a $750 bounty and a CVE was reserved.

I am submitting this report because the original Huntr disclosure workflow is no longer available and the CVE has not yet been published.

Please associate this report with CVE-2026-15367 rather than assigning a new CVE, unless the NLTK maintainers determine that the existing CVE does not correspond to this issue.

## Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: MERGED on develop. The load side is in every release since 3.9.4 (including v3.10.3); the save side is on develop and unreleased.

Fix commits: f2556f9e1 (load_maxent_params reads through open_datafile on a PathPointer whose open is pathsec.open; contained in tag 3.9.4 and every later tag) and 2a92b7182 (save_maxent_params validates tab_dir and writes every parameter file through pathsec.open), PR #3759 "Harden maxent / named-entity model-artifact saves against shared-tmp planting", merged 2026-08-18, merge commit a167e94bc on develop.

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_59f9_gqg8_mqpj.py, added on the open PR #3753 (head da55cab0e at the time of this note; measured on its earlier head 238f81500) together with commit 15f84f036 (load_maxent_params accepts a plain str or Path through FileSystemPathPointer). Verdict on 238f81500: FIXED (save and load outside every data root refused by pathsec). The same probe run against develop 2fa3f48fe reports the save refused and a PathPointer load refused, while a str or Path tab_dir raises AttributeError before any file is opened (the probe counts that crash as not fixed; no file is read or written).

cves.summary: TrendMicro ScanMail for Exchange 3.5 Evaluation allows a local attacker to recover the administrative credentials for ScanMail via a combination of unprotected registry keys and weakly encrypted passwords.
Directory traversal vulnerability in kpf for KDE 3.0.1 through KDE 3.0.3a allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files as the kpf user via a URL with a modified icon parameter.
Multiple buffer overflows in Heimdal before 0.5, possibly in both the (1) kadmind and (2) kdc servers, may allow remote attackers to gain root access.

Unknown vulnerabilities in Heimdal before 0.5 with unknown impact, possibly in the (1) kadmind and (2) kdc servers, may allow remote or local attackers to gain root or other access, but not via buffer overflows (CVE-2002-1225).
PAM 0.76 treats a disabled password as if it were an empty (null) password, which allows local and remote attackers to gain privileges as disabled users.

Adobe Acrobat Reader (acroread) 6, under certain circumstances when running with the "Certified plug-ins only" option disabled, loads plug-ins with signatures used for older versions of Acrobat, which can allow attackers to cause Acrobat to enter Certified mode and run untrusted plugins by modifying the CTIsCertifiedMode function.

The Name Service Daemon (nsd), when running on an NIS master on SGI IRIX 6.5.x through 6.5.20f, and possibly earlier versions, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via a UDP port scan.
Buffer overflow in Gaim 0.10.3 and earlier using the OSCAR protocol allows remote attackers to conduct a denial of service and possibly execute arbitrary commands via a long HTML tag.

The scripts (1) createdir.php, (2) removedir.php and (3) uploadfile.php for ezContents 1.41 and earlier do not check credentials, which allows remote attackers to create or delete directories and upload files via a direct HTTP POST request.
Buffer overflow in Novell GroupWise 6.0.1 Support Pack 1 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a long RCPT TO command.
rwcgi60 CGI program in Oracle Reports Server, by design, provides sensitive information such as the full pathname, which could enable remote attackers to use the information in additional attacks.

agent-zero 1.7, 1.8, 1.9, and 1.10 is vulnerable to Directory Traversal in python/helpers/file_browser.py:FileBrowser.__init__. The FileBrowser class initializes with the host root directory as the workspace, allowing the agent to access any file on the system without restriction.

NcFTP client 3.1.6 and 3.1.7, when the username and password are included in an FTP URL that is provided on the command line, allows local users to obtain sensitive information via "ps aux," which displays the URL in the process list.

Internet Explorer 5.5 allows remote attackers to bypass security restrictions via malformed URLs that contain dotless IP addresses, which causes Internet Explorer to process the page in the Intranet Zone, which may have fewer security restrictions, aka the "Zone Spoofing Vulnerability variant" of CVE-2001-0664.

Buffer overflow in the debug functionality in fp30reg.dll of Microsoft FrontPage Server Extensions (FPSE) 2000 and 2002 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a crafted chunked encoded request.

Unknown vulnerability in the SmartHTML interpreter (shtml.dll) in Microsoft FrontPage Server Extensions 2000 and 2002, and Microsoft SharePoint Team Services 2002, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (response failure) via a certain request.

The Windows Internet Naming Service (WINS) in Windows NT Server 4.0 SP 6a, NT Terminal Server 4.0 SP 6, Windows 2000 Server SP3 and SP4, and Windows Server 2003 does not properly validate the computer name value in a WINS packet, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (server crash), which results in an "unchecked buffer" and possibly triggers a buffer overflow, aka the "Name Validation Vulnerability."

The tcp_find_option function of the netfilter subsystem for IPv6 in the SUSE Linux 2.6.5 kernel with USAGI patches, when using iptables and TCP options rules, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (CPU consumption by infinite loop) via a large option length that produces a negative integer after a casting operation to the char type, a similar flaw to CVE-2004-0626.

Buffer overflow in the KSDWRTB function in the dbms_system package (dbms_system.ksdwrt) for Oracle 9i Database Server Release 2 9.2.0.3 and 9.2.0.4, 9i Release 1 9.0.1.4 and 9.0.1.5, and 8i Release 1 8.1.7.4, allows remote authorized users to execute arbitrary code via a long second argument.
Buffer overflow in uustat in Sun Solaris 8 and 9 allows local users to execute arbitrary code via a long -S command line argument.

Windows 2000 Server allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service by sending a continuous stream of binary zeros to various TCP and UDP ports, which significantly increases the CPU utilization.

## Original Description
Improper neutralization of special elements in data query logic in the GridFS component of the MongoDB Python Driver can cause a caller-supplied structured file identifier to be interpreted as a query condition rather than as a literal identifier. An authenticated user who can influence the identifier passed by an affected application may obtain stored file content beyond the intended target or cause all GridFS file chunks in the affected bucket to be removed, rendering stored file content unreadable. The affected rename operation may also rename a stored file other than the intended target.

abuse.console in Red Hat 2.1 uses relative pathnames to find and execute the undrv program, which allows local users to execute arbitrary commands via a path that points to a Trojan horse program.
The permissions for a system-critical NIS+ table (e.g. passwd) are inappropriate.
Vulnerability in a kernel error handling routine in SCO OpenServer 5.0.2 and earlier, and SCO Internet FastStart 1.0, allows local users to gain root privileges.
The suidperl and sperl program do not give up root privileges when changing UIDs back to the original users, allowing root access.
The dip program on many Linux systems allows local users to gain root access via a buffer overflow.
Local user gains root privileges via buffer overflow in rdist, via lookup() function.

The IRC component of Trillian 0.73 and 0.74 allows remote malicious IRC servers to cause a denial of service (crash) via a PART message with (1) a missing channel or (2) a channel that the Trillian user is not in.
